doc.title: Arthur Baron interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, June 3, 2020 [interview 2 of 2]

title: Calling Black friends to stand with them, and white privilege
summary: Baron and his wife Ingvild phone Black friends; he reflects on playing with Black musicians and on privilege.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: Well, as I told you earlier, my wife who is also a Caucasian from Norway, who has never seen anything like this except on the news, and she doesn’t want to march, and I understand it because it’s really dangerous with the virus too, and I’ve got my feelings about that, I’m not sure, but she worked on it yesterday and she came home and told me, and she’s a bit shy, she gave me an idea that she wanted me to initiate, and I would have initiated it but I really wanted her to. She said, “Let’s call up all our black or Afro- American friends” —it’s so hard to know what to say, but I think either is acceptable now — “and tell them that we stand with them. And bring the conversation up to another level, bring the relationship up to another level. And you know what? We called several of our friends. I’m very lucky, I played with Stevie Wonder, Duke Ellington, B.B. King, other black groups you know? Jon Faddis used to say to me, “Why don’t you play with your own kind?” And I’ve learned a whole lot. I can never know what it’s like to be in the skin of a black man but I can see what it’s like and I’ve seen — and this color of our skin is like, what’s the word I’m looking for, we have a leg up.
Yeah, we have a path sort of.
Yeah but there’s a great word, white —
